records.topic: Why QR Codes Have Three Corner Squares
records.title: Why QR Codes Have Three Corner Squares
records.coreQuestion: Why does every QR code have three large squares in its corners?
records.hook: Those three QR squares aren't decoration.
records.openingLine: Those three QR squares aren't decoration.
records.secondBeat: They tell the scanner where to look.
records.mechanism: The corner squares are position detection patterns that let a reader find the code and its orientation
records.expectedConsequence: A scanner can find and orient the code from any angle, so reading is fast
records.misconception: The squares look like a logo or styling, but they are the locating pattern the reader searches for.
records.payoff: The squares use a black-and-white ratio chosen because it is rare on printed matter.
editorialTitles: Why QR Codes Have Three Corner Squares
The Hidden Job of the Squares on Every QR Code
Those QR Code Squares Aren't Decoration
visualScenes: a real QR code on a product label
macro view of one corner square
labelled position detection pattern
stripe-ratio diagram across one square
phone scanning the code at a tilted angle

narration.text: Those three QR squares aren't decoration.
They tell the scanner where to look.
Denso Wave released the QR Code in 1994, and QR means quick response.
The corner marks are position detection patterns. Finding them made high-speed reading possible.
Why squares? The team said that pattern was least likely to appear on business forms.
They surveyed flyers, magazines and cardboard boxes for the rarest black-and-white ratio.
That rare ratio lets a scanner orient the code from any angle.

facts.claim: Denso Wave, then a division of Denso Corporation, announced the release of the QR Code in 1994.
facts.quote: In 1994, DENSO WAVE (then a division of DENSO CORPORATION) announced the release of its QR Code
facts.source: DENSO WAVE — History of QR Code

facts.claim: QR stands for quick response, reflecting a development focus on high-speed reading.
facts.quote: The QR in the name stands for quick response
facts.source: DENSO WAVE — History of QR Code

facts.claim: The developers added positional information indicating that a code is present and should be read.
facts.quote: adding positional information indicating the existence of a code to be read
facts.source: DENSO WAVE — History of QR Code

facts.claim: The square position detection marks made high-speed reading possible.
facts.quote: By incorporating these marks into their code, high-speed reading became possible
facts.source: DENSO WAVE — History of QR Code

facts.claim: Masahiro Hara said square marks were chosen because that pattern was least likely to appear on business forms.
facts.quote: it was the pattern least likely to appear on various business forms and the like
facts.source: DENSO WAVE — History of QR Code

facts.claim: A similar-looking mark near the code could be mistaken for a position detection pattern, so the pattern had to be unique.
facts.quote: their position detection patterns had to be truly unique
facts.source: DENSO WAVE — History of QR Code

facts.claim: The team surveyed the ratio of white to black areas in printing on fliers, magazines and cardboard boxes.
facts.quote: an exhaustive survey of the ratio of white to black areas in pictures and symbols printed on fliers, magazines, cardboard boxes
facts.source: DENSO WAVE — History of QR Code

facts.claim: The least-used black-and-white ratio on printed matter, 1:1:3:1:1, set the widths of the position detection patterns.
facts.quote: came up with the least used ratio of black and white areas on printed matter. This ratio was 1:1:3:1:1
facts.source: DENSO WAVE — History of QR Code

facts.claim: Searching for this unique ratio lets a reader determine the code's orientation at any scanning angle.
facts.quote: the orientation of their code could be determined regardless of the angle of scanning
facts.source: DENSO WAVE — History of QR Code

facts.claim: The QR code was invented by Masahiro Hara of Denso Wave for labelling automobile parts.
facts.quote: invented in 1994 by Masahiro Hara of the Japanese company Denso Wave for labelling automobile parts
facts.source: Wikipedia — QR code

facts.claim: The three finder patterns sit at the upper left, upper right and lower left corners.
facts.quote: at the upper left, upper right and lower left corners of the QR code image
facts.source: Wikipedia — QR code

sources.name: DENSO WAVE — History of QR Code
DENSO WAVE — What is a QR Code?

records.topic: Why the Bluetooth Logo Looks Like That
records.title: Why the Bluetooth Logo Looks Like That
records.coreQuestion: Why is the Bluetooth logo that angular symbol, and where did the name come from?
records.hook: The Bluetooth logo is a Viking king's initials.
records.openingLine: The Bluetooth logo is a Viking king's initials.
records.secondBeat: Two runes, merged into one symbol.
records.mechanism: The logo is a bind rune that merges the Younger Futhark runes for Harald Bluetooth's initials
records.expectedConsequence: A temporary code name became the permanent name and logo of a global wireless standard
records.misconception: Bluetooth sounds like a technical acronym, but it is a king's nickname that was meant to be a placeholder.
records.payoff: The symbol is Harald's initials, written in runes.
editorialTitles: Why the Bluetooth Logo Looks Like That
The Bluetooth Logo Is a Viking King's Initials
Bluetooth Was Never Meant to Be the Name
Bluetooth Was Only a Placeholder Name
The Viking King Hidden in the Bluetooth Logo
Why Bluetooth Is Named After a King
The Runes Inside the Bluetooth Logo
Bluetooth Almost Became RadioWire or PAN
The Code Name That Became Bluetooth
visualScenes: the Bluetooth logo on a phone settings screen
the two runes drawn separately
the runes sliding together into the logo
a runestone carving
a laptop and phone pairing

narration.text: The Bluetooth logo is a Viking king's initials.
Two runes, merged into one symbol.
The name honours King Harald Bluetooth, who united Denmark and Norway.
At an industry meeting, Intel's Jim Kardach suggested it as a temporary code name.
Harald united Scandinavia. This radio link would unite PCs and phones.
It was only a placeholder. RadioWire or PAN was meant to replace it.
PAN was already everywhere online, and RadioWire's trademark check ran out of time.
So the logo merges Harald's initials in runes: H and B.

facts.claim: King Harald Bluetooth Gormsson was known for uniting Denmark and Norway in 958.
facts.quote: Uniting Denmark and Norway in 958
facts.source: Bluetooth SIG — Origin of the Name

facts.claim: Harald's nickname came from a dead tooth of a dark blue-grey colour.
facts.quote: His dead tooth, which was a dark blue/grey color, and earned him the nickname Bluetooth
facts.source: Bluetooth SIG — Origin of the Name

facts.claim: In 1996 Intel, Ericsson and Nokia met to plan the standardization of a short-range radio technology.
facts.quote: In 1996, three industry leaders, Intel, Ericsson, and Nokia, met to plan the standardization of this short-range radio technology
facts.source: Bluetooth SIG — Origin of the Name

facts.claim: At that meeting Jim Kardach of Intel suggested Bluetooth as a temporary code name.
facts.quote: Jim Kardach from Intel suggested Bluetooth as a temporary code name
facts.source: Bluetooth SIG — Origin of the Name

facts.claim: Kardach compared Harald uniting Scandinavia with uniting the PC and cellular industries through a short-range wireless link.
facts.quote: was famous for uniting Scandinavia just as we intended to unite the PC and cellular industries with a short-range wireless link
facts.source: Bluetooth SIG — Origin of the Name

facts.claim: Bluetooth was intended only as a placeholder name.
facts.quote: Bluetooth was only intended as a placeholder until marketing could come up with something really cool
facts.source: Bluetooth SIG — Origin of the Name

facts.claim: The planned replacement names were RadioWire or PAN (Personal Area Networking).
facts.quote: Bluetooth was to be replaced with either RadioWire or PAN (Personal Area Networking)
facts.source: Bluetooth SIG — Origin of the Name

facts.claim: PAN already had tens of thousands of hits on the internet.
facts.quote: PAN was the front runner, but an exhaustive search discovered it already had tens of thousands of hits throughout the internet
facts.source: Bluetooth SIG — Origin of the Name

facts.claim: A full trademark search on RadioWire could not be completed in time for launch.
facts.quote: A full trademark search on RadioWire couldn't be completed in time for launch, making Bluetooth the only choice
facts.source: Bluetooth SIG — Origin of the Name

facts.claim: The Bluetooth logo is a bind rune merging the Younger Futhark runes Hagall and Bjarkan, Harald's initials.
facts.quote: The Bluetooth logo is a bind rune merging the Younger Futhark runes
facts.source: Bluetooth SIG — Origin of the Name

facts.claim: Kardach proposed the code name after seeing a picture of Harald Bluetooth's runestone in a history of the Vikings.
facts.quote: Upon discovering a picture of the runestone of Harald Bluetooth in the book A History of the Vikings by Gwyn Jones
facts.source: Wikipedia — Bluetooth

sources.name: Bluetooth SIG — Origin of the Name

records.topic: Why Some Barcode Bars Are Longer
records.title: Why Some Barcode Bars Are Longer
records.coreQuestion: Why are a few bars on a UPC barcode longer than the rest?
records.hook: Some barcode bars are longer, and that's deliberate.
records.openingLine: Some barcode bars are longer, and that's deliberate.
records.secondBeat: They hold no number at all.
records.mechanism: The longer start, middle and end guard bars encode no digit; they mark the label, split the digits and set the timing for the scanner
records.expectedConsequence: A scanner can detect the label and tell which half it is reading
records.misconception: Every stripe looks like data, but the longest bars carry no digit.
records.payoff: The longest bars are signposts for the scanner, not data.
editorialTitles: Why Some Barcode Bars Are Longer
The Barcode Bars That Hold No Number
Look Closely at a Barcode's Longest Bars
visualScenes: a UPC barcode on a grocery item
macro view of the longer guard bars
labelled start, middle and end guard patterns
the two six-digit halves highlighted
a checkout scanner reading the code

narration.text: Some barcode bars are longer, and that's deliberate.
They hold no number at all.
On a UPC barcode, the start, middle and end guard bars extend lower.
They encode no digit; they split the code into two halves.
IBM's George Laurer was assigned to design a supermarket scanner label.
His team defined guard bars so a scanner could detect the label.
They even told it which half it was reading.
So the longest bars are signposts, not data.

facts.claim: The start, middle and end guard bars of a UPC-A barcode extend further down than the digit bars.
facts.quote: The bars forming the S (start), M (middle), and E (end) guard patterns, are extended downwards
facts.source: Wikipedia — Universal Product Code

facts.claim: Guard patterns do not encode a digit; they help decoding.
facts.quote: not encoding a digit) are intermixed to help decoding
facts.source: Wikipedia — Universal Product Code

facts.claim: The guard patterns separate the two groups of six digits and establish the timing.
facts.quote: The guard patterns separate the two groups of six numerical digits and establish the timing
facts.source: Wikipedia — Universal Product Code

facts.claim: A UPC-A barcode has exactly 30 bars: 6 form guard patterns and 24 represent its 12 digits.
facts.quote: all UPC-A barcodes consist of exactly (3 × 2) + (12 × 2) = 30 bars, of which 6 represent guard patterns and 24 represent numerical digits
facts.source: Wikipedia — Universal Product Code

facts.claim: IBM assigned George Laurer to determine how to make a supermarket scanner and label.
facts.quote: assigned George Laurer to determine how to make a supermarket scanner and label
facts.source: Wikipedia — Universal Product Code

facts.claim: Laurer and a colleague defined guard bars and how a scanner should detect the label.
facts.quote: Together they defined guard bars and a definition of how to detect the label
facts.source: Wikipedia — Universal Product Code

facts.claim: The guard bars also identified which half of the label was being read and trained the scanner's threshold circuits.
facts.quote: The guard bars also provided identification for half label discrimination and training bars for the scanner threshold circuits
facts.source: Wikipedia — Universal Product Code

facts.claim: Splitting the label into two halves allowed the bars to be cut nearly in half in length.
facts.quote: suggested if the label were split into two halves the bar lengths could be cut nearly in half
facts.source: Wikipedia — Universal Product Code

facts.claim: The first UPC-marked item scanned at a retail checkout was Wrigley's Juicy Fruit gum in Troy, Ohio, on 26 June 1974.
facts.quote: Wrigley's Juicy Fruit chewing gum, purchased at the Marsh supermarket in Troy, Ohio
facts.source: Wikipedia — Universal Product Code

sources.name: GS1 US — UPCs, barcodes and prefixes

records.topic: The Shopping Cart Started as a Folding Chair
records.title: The Shopping Cart Started as a Folding Chair
records.coreQuestion: Where did the shopping cart come from, and why did shoppers first refuse to use it?
records.hook: The shopping cart started as a folding chair.
records.openingLine: The shopping cart started as a folding chair.
records.secondBeat: And shoppers first refused to push it.
records.mechanism: Sylvan Goldman put a basket on a folding chair's seat and wheels on its legs to let customers move more groceries
records.expectedConsequence: After demonstrations by hired models, shopping carts became extremely popular
records.misconception: The cart seems like an obvious idea, but shoppers initially resisted it.
records.payoff: A folding chair with wheels became the shopping cart.
editorialTitles: The Shopping Cart Started as a Folding Chair
Why Shoppers First Refused the Shopping Cart
The Folding Chair Behind Every Shopping Cart
visualScenes: a modern shopping cart in an aisle
a wooden folding chair
a basket placed on the chair seat with wheels on the legs
the 1930s folding basket carrier
a row of carts nested together

narration.text: The shopping cart started as a folding chair.
And shoppers first refused to push it.
In 1936, grocer Sylvan Goldman wondered how customers could move more groceries.
He put a basket on a folding chair's seat and wheels on its legs.
His Humpty Dumpty stores introduced these folding basket carriers in 1937.
One offended woman told him she had pushed her last baby.
So Goldman hired models to push the carts around his store.
After that, the folding chair on wheels became extremely popular.

facts.quote: in 1936, Goldman sat in his office wondering how customers might move more groceries
facts.source: Wikipedia — Shopping cart

facts.claim: Goldman put a basket on the seat of a wooden folding chair and wheels on its legs.
facts.quote: He found a wooden folding chair and put a basket on the seat and wheels on the legs
facts.source: Wikipedia — Shopping cart

facts.quote: Goldman called his carts "folding basket carriers"
facts.source: Wikipedia — Shopping cart

facts.claim: One of the first shopping carts was introduced on June 4, 1937, by Goldman, owner of the Humpty Dumpty supermarket chain in Oklahoma.
facts.quote: One of the first shopping carts was introduced on June 4, 1937, the invention of Sylvan Goldman
facts.source: Wikipedia — Shopping cart

facts.claim: An offended woman told Goldman she had pushed her last baby.
facts.quote: an offended woman informed Goldman
facts.source: Wikipedia — Shopping cart

facts.claim: Goldman hired male and female models to push carts around the store, and carts then became extremely popular.
facts.quote: Goldman hired several male and female models to push his new invention around his store
facts.source: Wikipedia — Shopping cart

facts.claim: Goldman and his mechanic Fred Young began tinkering with the design.
facts.quote: Goldman and one of his employees, a mechanic named Fred Young, began tinkering
facts.source: Wikipedia — Shopping cart

facts.claim: Orla Watson invented the swinging rear door that allows carts to nest, in 1946.
facts.quote: Orla Watson, who invented the swinging rear door to allow for "nesting" in 1946
facts.source: Wikipedia — Shopping cart

facts.claim: Goldman established the Folding Basket Carrier Company to manufacture his invention.
facts.quote: He established the Folding Basket Carrier Company to manufacture his invention

records.topic: Why Road Cat's Eyes Clean Themselves
records.title: Why Road Cat's Eyes Clean Themselves
records.coreQuestion: How do cat's eye road studs keep their reflectors clean?
records.hook: Road cat's eyes clean themselves when cars hit them.
records.openingLine: Road cat's eyes clean themselves when cars hit them.
records.secondBeat: The trick is a rubber eyelid.
records.mechanism: Traffic presses the flexible rubber dome down and a fixed rubber wiper cleans the reflectors as they sink
records.expectedConsequence: Passing traffic keeps the reflectors clean
records.misconception: They look like simple glass beads, but the stud is a small cleaning mechanism.
records.payoff: Every car that drives over a cat's eye helps clean it.
editorialTitles: Why Road Cat's Eyes Clean Themselves
The Hidden Wiper Inside Every Road Stud
Cars Clean These Road Reflectors
The Rubber Eyelid Inside Cat's Eyes
How Road Studs Wipe Their Own Reflectors
Percy Shaw's Self-Cleaning Road Stud
Why Traffic Keeps Cat's Eyes Clean
The 1934 Road Stud That Cleans Itself
Rain Makes These Road Reflectors Cleaner
What Happens When a Tyre Hits a Cat's Eye
visualScenes: cat's eyes glowing on a night road
macro view of a road stud
cutaway of the rubber dome and wiper

rainwater pooled in the stud base

narration.text: Road cat's eyes clean themselves when cars hit them.
The trick is a rubber eyelid.
Percy Shaw of Halifax patented reflective road studs in 1934.
The name came from a cat's eyes reflecting light in the dark.
The reflectors sit in a flexible rubber dome inside a cast iron housing.
When a tyre presses it down, a fixed rubber wiper cleans the reflectors.
Rainwater held in the base makes that wipe even more efficient.
So passing traffic keeps the reflectors clean.

facts.quote: Reflective Cats Eye road studs were patented by Percy Shaw of Halifax in 1934
facts.source: National Motor Museum — When were Cats Eyes first invented?

facts.claim: A company to manufacture the studs was established in 1935.
facts.quote: A manufacturing company, Reflective Road Studs Ltd, was established in 1935
facts.source: National Motor Museum — When were Cats Eyes first invented?

facts.claim: The name came from Shaw's inspiration: eyeshine reflecting from a cat's eyes.
facts.quote: the eyeshine reflecting from the eyes of a cat
facts.source: Wikipedia — Cat's eye (road)

facts.claim: The original design set two pairs of retroreflectors into a white rubber dome mounted in a cast iron housing.
facts.quote: two pairs of retroreflectors set into a white rubber dome, mounted in a cast iron housing
facts.source: Wikipedia — Cat's eye (road)

facts.claim: The flexible rubber dome is deformed by passing traffic.
facts.quote: the flexible rubber dome which is occasionally deformed by the passage of traffic
facts.source: Wikipedia — Cat's eye (road)

facts.claim: A fixed rubber wiper cleans the reflectors as they sink below the road surface.
facts.quote: A fixed rubber wiper cleans the surface of the reflectors as they sink below the surface of the road
facts.source: Wikipedia — Cat's eye (road)

facts.claim: The base holds water after rain, making the cleaning more efficient.
facts.quote: the base tends to hold water after a shower of rain, making this process even more efficient
facts.source: Wikipedia — Cat's eye (road)

facts.claim: The rubber cushion collected rainwater and closed like an eyelid over the glass when a tyre ran over it.
facts.quote: closed like an eyelid over the glass stud when a car tyre ran over it
facts.source: MyLearning — Percy Shaw, the Inventor of Catseyes

facts.claim: Metal kerbs protect the dome and give tactile and audible feedback to drivers who wander.
facts.quote: which also give tactile and audible feedback for wandering drivers
facts.source: Wikipedia — Cat's eye (road)

records.title: Why Jeans Have Copper Rivets
records.coreQuestion: Why do jeans have small copper rivets at the pocket corners?
records.hook: Those copper dots on jeans started on horse blankets.
records.openingLine: Those copper dots on jeans started on horse blankets.
records.secondBeat: A tailor borrowed them for work trousers.
records.mechanism: Rivets reinforce stress points such as pocket corners that tore apart under heavy wear
records.expectedConsequence: Riveted work trousers became the blue jean; back-pocket rivets were later covered and then removed
records.misconception: The rivets look decorative, but they began as reinforcement borrowed from horse blankets.
records.payoff: Rivets still reinforce the most vulnerable parts of jeans.
editorialTitles: Why Jeans Have Copper Rivets
The Horse-Blanket Trick Hiding on Your Jeans
Why Jeans Lost Their Back-Pocket Rivets
visualScenes: copper rivets on a jeans pocket
macro view of one rivet
a riveted horse blanket corner
an 1873 patent drawing
a back pocket without rivets

narration.text: Those copper dots on jeans started on horse blankets.
A tailor borrowed them for work trousers.
In Reno, tailor Jacob Davis used rivets on pocket corners that tore apart.
He couldn't afford a patent, so he asked Levi Strauss to apply with him.
In 1873 they patented an improvement in fastening pocket openings.
But back-pocket rivets scratched furniture and saddles.
From 1937 they were covered, and by 1966 they were gone.
The rivets you see now still guard the most vulnerable spots.

facts.claim: Jacob Davis pioneered rivets on work trousers in 1871 while working as a tailor in Reno, Nevada.
facts.quote: Jacob Davis pioneered rivets while working as a tailor in Reno
facts.source: Levi Strauss & Co. Archives — Those Oft-Forgotten Pant Parts

facts.claim: Davis had originally used rivets on horse blankets.
facts.quote: Davis had originally used rivets on horse blankets
facts.source: Levi Strauss & Co. Archives — Those Oft-Forgotten Pant Parts

facts.claim: Rivets reinforced stress points such as back-pocket corners and the crotch, which often tore apart under heavy wear.
facts.quote: particularly the corners of the back pockets and the crotch, which often tore apart when exposed to heavy duty wear and tear
facts.source: Levi Strauss & Co. Archives — Those Oft-Forgotten Pant Parts

facts.claim: Davis did not have the money to patent the technique, so he asked Levi Strauss to apply with him.
facts.quote: Since Davis did not have the money required to patent the technique of using rivets
facts.source: Levi Strauss & Co. Archives — Those Oft-Forgotten Pant Parts

facts.claim: In 1873 the pair received a patent for an improvement in fastening pocket openings.
facts.quote: the pair received a patent for “improvement in fastening pocket-openings.”
facts.source: Levi Strauss & Co. Archives — Those Oft-Forgotten Pant Parts

facts.claim: Copper rivets kept pockets from ripping and made the openings stronger.
facts.quote: Copper rivets kept the pockets from ripping and made the openings stronger and more secure
facts.source: Levi Strauss & Co. Archives — Pockets Full of History

facts.claim: In 1937 Levi's began covering back-pocket rivets because the copper points scratched furniture and saddles.
facts.quote: many had issues with the copper points scratching furniture and saddles
facts.source: Levi Strauss & Co. Archives — Pockets Full of History

facts.claim: The covered back-pocket rivets were dropped altogether by 1966 because they wore through the denim.
facts.quote: by 1966 were ditched altogether because they continued to wear through even the toughest denim
facts.source: Levi Strauss & Co. Archives — Pockets Full of History

facts.claim: Rivets continue to strengthen the most vulnerable parts of jeans.
facts.quote: rivets continue to strengthen and reinforce the most vulnerable parts of our jeans
facts.source: Levi Strauss & Co. Archives — Those Oft-Forgotten Pant Parts

sources.name: Levi Strauss & Co. Archives — Those Oft-Forgotten Pant Parts
Levi Strauss & Co. Archives — Pockets Full of History
